title: Fluent is not the same as true

sections.skill: Explain why fluent language is not evidence

questions.prompt: Why do language model answers usually sound smooth and confident?

choices.text: They have checked every fact before writing
They copy only from verified textbooks
They are always written by human experts
They are trained to produce natural-sounding text

questions.correct_answer: They are trained to produce natural-sounding text
questions.intro: Language models are trained to produce text that reads naturally, so their answers are usually FLUENT: smooth, confident and well organized. Fluency is not EVIDENCE. A model can describe a book that does not exist, invent a statistic, or misstate a rule in the same confident tone it uses for correct facts. Signs such as precise numbers, formal language or phrases like "studies show" do not prove anything by themselves. To judge a claim, look for something you can check: a source you can open, a calculation you can redo, or a fact you can confirm elsewhere.
questions.feedback: Fluency comes from training on natural text.

sections.skill: Separate how a claim sounds from what supports it

questions.prompt: Which part tells you whether to trust a claim?

choices.text: How long it is
What supports it
How formal the words are
How confident it sounds

questions.correct_answer: What supports it
questions.intro: Two questions help with any claim. First: HOW DOES IT SOUND? Confident, formal, detailed, friendly. Second: WHAT SUPPORTS IT? A source you can open, a calculation you can redo, a fact you can confirm elsewhere. Only the second question tells you whether to trust it. Example: "The museum opens at 9 a.m., according to its website (link)" has support you can check. "The museum definitely opens at 9 a.m." only sounds sure. A claim can sound weak and be true, or sound strong and be false.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Check the claims that matter in a mixed answer

questions.prompt: An answer ends with "This is a verified fact." What does that sentence add?

choices.text: No evidence; it is also generated text
Proof that a person verified it first
A legal guarantee of accuracy
A link to the verification

questions.correct_answer: No evidence; it is also generated text
questions.intro: Some answers include their own reassurances, such as "I am confident," "this is a verified fact," or a neat reference list. These are still generated text, so they do not add evidence by themselves. An answer can also mix correct and incorrect parts, which makes errors harder to notice: three right facts can make a fourth wrong one seem trustworthy. A practical habit is to identify the specific claims that matter for your decision and check those, rather than judging the whole answer by how it sounds.

questions.prompt: An answer gives four facts; you confirm three are right. What should you assume about the fourth?

It must be right since the others were
Nothing yet; check it too if it matters
